representativeSnapshot.kind: Static review of the full staff_members policy history in the active chain, plus executed behavioural evidence on a throwaway PostgreSQL 16.15 cluster. The defect named by CP-104 is real at 20250818120000:361-362 (read_all_staff, SELECT USING auth.role() = 'authenticated'), :395-396 (insert_staff, INSERT WITH CHECK) and :426-427 (update_staff, UPDATE USING). MEASURED CORRECTION TO THE FINDING, which changes what the operator must probe: on a target where the whole chain has been replayed in order, those three policies are ALREADY ABSENT. 20260823210000_harden_hiring_onboarding_pii.sql names read_all_staff literally in its v_permissive array (:263) and catches insert_staff and update_staff in its 'literally authenticated can do anything' sweep (:300-315), and the same file creates staff_members_employer_manage_hiring (:352-364) keyed on employer_entity_type / employer_entity_id. Both drops are dynamic execute format(...) calls, which is why a literal grep for 'drop policy ... on staff_members' does not see them. The migration is still required, for three measured reasons: (1) DB-002 recorded that some hosted versions were applied by raw Management API SQL, so 'the chain says it was dropped' is not evidence the target dropped it; (2) can_manage_hiring returns false for a null entity type or id (20260625000000:203-205), so the org-scoped event/tour staffing rows 20260821031214 was written for are reachable only by the worker themselves; (3) no org-scoped policy for staff_members exists anywhere in the chain, while the sibling table staff_shifts has four. Executed evidence: 61 PASS / 0 FAIL in supabase/tests/db013_staff_members_scope.harness.sh, including a real negative control (an authenticated non-member reads 5 of 5 rows, inserts into org A and updates org A's row BEFORE the migration) and the measured denial after it.

assumptions: `authenticated` holds table-level SELECT on `public.organizations`. The three new policies resolve `org_id` through an RLS-evaluated EXISTS on that table, so the grant is load-bearing. Supabase's default privileges grant it and the chain does not manage table grants in SQL, so this is not verifiable from the chain - the same premise the 20260926140000 manifest already records for `anon` on `post_likes`. The failure direction is safe: if the grant were absent the policies DENY, they never open. The operator manifest carries it as a preflight probe rather than as an assumption the lane can discharge.

RFC 9457 aside: this is a SECURITY DEFINER helper, not a row-level policy, so its EXECUTE grants are irrelevant here. `public.has_perm` was granted to authenticated, anon and service_role by 20260711153040:37-38 and DB-002 found that pattern flagged; DB-002's 20260914090000 migration revokes PUBLIC/anon, and this lane did not assume that revocation had landed. The policies call has_perm through the caller, not through a definer wrapper, so the RLS decision is made for the calling role either way.

`org_role_permissions` is NOT seeded with `workforce.view` or `workforce.manage` by this migration. The chain seeds `owner`, `admin`, `production`, `finance` (20250816132000:44-48) and `tour_manager` (20260712005429:219-233) with the older `staff.manage` / `event.manage` vocabulary; 20260821180438:81-95 added `workforce.*` only to the per-member `org_members.permissions` CHECK constraint. So with the chain's own matrix `has_perm(..., 'workforce.view')` is false for every seeded role and these three policies grant access only to a member row carrying `workforce.*` directly. That is fail-closed, it is what `staff_shifts_scoped_*` already shipped, and widening the role matrix is a workforce-identity-contract change owned by WFC-003 (CP-102), not a side effect of a security fix. It is raised as a report finding, not actioned here.

The read policy admits `workforce.manage` as well as `workforce.view`, which is WIDER than `staff_shifts_scoped_read`. This is deliberate and it is the same disjunction 20260903120000_site_map_zone_security_and_canonical_bridge.sql:782-783 already uses for a read policy in this chain. A roster manager who cannot read the roster is not a scope, and the historical response to that gap in this codebase is to add a permissive policy, which is the defect CP-104 describes.

`staff_members_employer_manage_hiring` is NOT dropped. It is a SCOPED policy, not a permissive one, and it is the live access path for the VEN-103 canonical venue roster, which is keyed on `employer_entity_type = 'venue'`. Because RLS policies are permissive and OR, keeping it means this migration is strictly additive to access: no committed surface can lose a row it could previously read, insert or update. The same OR is why the fix cannot be verified by reading the new policies alone - which is the whole of CP-104.
`staff_shifts` is explicitly out of scope and is not touched, not read and not in this diff. Its four `staff_shifts_scoped_*` policies are correct as shipped.

Every existing `staff_members` row is preserved. No table, column, index, trigger or function is created, altered or dropped; no data row is read for update or deleted. The only objects this file changes are policies.

`organizations.owner_id` is not created by any active migration, so `can_manage_hiring`'s organization-ownership fallback (20260625000000:343-347) cannot fire on a real target. The chain's only working organization path is `has_entity_permission` (20260823210100:87-129), which DB-002's 20260914090000 also revokes from anon. The behavioural harness exercises the employer-scoped survivor through the VENUE branch of `can_manage_hiring`, which is a real chain path and needs no RBAC graph.
layeredPlan: Layer 0 (preflight, read-only, operator). Run the Layer 0 queries in preflight.rowCountQueries and record the result. Three things decide whether this file is correct for THIS target: (a) which policy names are actually present on public.staff_members and what each one's `pg_get_expr` renders - if a differently-named role-permissive policy is on any of SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE, this migration does not remove it and the operator must stop and route it back; (b) `has_table_privilege('authenticated','public.organizations','select')` - if false, the three new policies will deny everything and org managers will lose the org-scoped view, so stop and report before applying; (c) the row counts, so the postflight comparison has a baseline.

Layer 1 (apply, single run, operator). One transaction, explicit, this file only - never `supabase db reset`, never `db push --include-all` (CP-051). DROP POLICY IF EXISTS on the three permissive names, CREATE POLICY on staff_members_scoped_read / _insert / _update, COMMENT ON POLICY on each, a guarded re-create of staff_members_worker_read_own only if absent, then a DO block that RAISES unless RLS is enabled, the three permissive names are gone, the four required policies exist on the right commands, no policy on the table carries an unconditional clause, and no policy on the table is reachable by anon or PUBLIC. The post-condition is inside the same transaction as the change, so a target that cannot reach the asserted state fails the apply rather than reporting success. No other migration is applied in the same run.

Layer 2 (postflight, read-only, operator). Run supabase/tests/db013_staff_members_org_scope_contract.sql; expect zero violation rows and exactly one summary row `DB-013 staff_members organization scope|t`. Then the real-caller probes in postflight.queries, as three DIFFERENT identities: an authenticated account with no membership in the owning organization (must read 0 rows, INSERT must fail 42501, UPDATE must match 0 rows), a member of the owning organization (must read the tenant's rows), and a worker whose own staff_members row has their `user_id` (must read exactly their own row and nothing else).

Layer 3 (no fourth layer in this lane). The two items the chain leaves open are NOT this migration's to fix and are routed rather than absorbed: the `workforce.*` role-matrix gap (WFC-003, CP-102) and the `staff_shifts_scoped_read` view-only predicate (recorded in the DB-013 report as a suspect for the orchestrator to route). Neither is required for this migration to be safe, and folding either in would widen DB-013 into a workforce-identity decision it is not sized for.

rowCountQueries: SELECT p.polname, p.polcmd, p.polpermissive, p.polroles::regrole[], pg_get_expr(p.polqual, p.polrelid) AS using_expr, pg_get_expr(p.polwithcheck, p.polrelid) AS check_expr FROM pg_policy p JOIN pg_class c ON c.oid = p.polrelid JOIN pg_namespace n ON n.oid = c.relnamespace WHERE n.nspname = 'public' AND c.relname = 'staff_members' ORDER BY p.polcmd, p.polname
SELECT count(*) AS staff_members_rows, count(*) FILTER (WHERE org_id IS NULL) AS null_org_rows, count(DISTINCT org_id) AS distinct_orgs FROM public.staff_members
SELECT c.relrowsecurity, c.relforcerowsecurity FROM pg_class c JOIN pg_namespace n ON n.oid = c.relnamespace WHERE n.nspname = 'public' AND c.relname = 'staff_members'
preflight.expectedAffectedRows: Zero data rows are changed. Three policy names are dropped if present, three policies are created, and staff_members_worker_read_own is created only if it is absent. No table, column, index, constraint, trigger or function is created, altered or dropped.

execution.resumeStrategy: Authored - manual apply pending (CP-051). One transaction, one file. CREATE POLICY and DROP POLICY take ACCESS EXCLUSIVE on the pg_class/pg_policy catalog rows, not on the table's data, and no table is rewritten or re-vacuumed, so there is no lock-budget risk from the data side. Safe to apply BEFORE any consumer change: because RLS policies are permissive and OR, and because staff_members_employer_manage_hiring and staff_members_worker_read_own are both retained, no committed surface loses a row it could previously read, insert or update. The only behaviour that changes is that a caller with no scope on an org can no longer read, insert or update that org's rows - which is the point of the change.
execution.idempotency: Deterministic and repeatable. DROP POLICY IF EXISTS on the three permissive names; DROP POLICY IF EXISTS + CREATE POLICY with a final name on each of the three scoped policies; COMMENT ON POLICY; a pg_policies-guarded create of staff_members_worker_read_own that is a no-op when it already exists; a DO block that only reads the catalog and RAISEs. Verified by applying the file twice on a throwaway PostgreSQL 16.15 cluster in supabase/tests/db013_staff_members_scope.harness.sh: the second apply produced no error and the surviving policy set was byte-identical, measured as staff_members_employer_manage_hiring,staff_members_scoped_insert,staff_members_scoped_read,staff_members_scoped_update,staff_members_worker_read_own before and after.

quarantine.strategy: No data movement, no backfill, no batch. The change is six policy objects. There is no partial-application state: the file is one transaction and its own post-condition RAISEs if the asserted state is unreachable, so a half-applied policy set cannot be committed.
quarantine.lockBudget: The `exists` conjunct on public.organizations is a primary-key lookup per candidate row, executed as the calling role, and `has_perm` is wrapped in `(select ...)` exactly as 20260821031214 does so the planner evaluates it once per statement rather than once per row. staff_members has `staff_members_org_idx` (20260821031214:37-38) as a partial index on org_id, so a scoped read is an index range scan, not a table scan. The added EXISTS is not a new access pattern for the planner - a SECURITY DEFINER is_org_member call against org_members(org_id) was already the shape of the organizations SELECT policy every org-scoped query already traverses.

constraints: No constraint is added, altered or dropped. `staff_members_org_id_fkey` (20260821031214:5, ON DELETE SET NULL) and `staff_shifts_requires_scope` are untouched.

The three new policies ARE the authorization boundary. `staff_members_scoped_read` requires a non-null org_id, an org_id that resolves to a public.organizations row, and workforce.view or workforce.manage on it. `staff_members_scoped_insert` requires the same with workforce.manage. `staff_members_scoped_update` requires it on BOTH using and with check, so a manager of org B can neither read-modify-write a row of org A nor re-scope an org A row into org B.

`staff_members_worker_read_own` is NOT dropped and NOT replaced. It is re-created only when absent, guarded on the `user_id` column existing, using the same `pg_policies` existence guard 20260625000000:497-514 used. An existing definition is left byte-identical, so a worker keeps reading their own row and nothing about that policy changes.

`staff_members_employer_manage_hiring` is left in place and is not an unauthorized-policy violation under the contract test's check 9: it is SCOPED, keyed on employer_entity_type / employer_entity_id through the SECURITY DEFINER can_manage_hiring, which returns false for a null entity type or id. It is enumerated in the contract test's allow-list by name so that any OTHER survivor is reported rather than assumed benign.
indexes: No index is added. The new policies add a primary-key EXISTS on public.organizations per candidate row plus the has_perm call, both of which sit behind `staff_members_org_idx` (partial on org_id, 20260821031214:37-38) for the read path and after the row is located for the write path.
constraintsAndIndexes.validationPlan: supabase/tests/db013_staff_members_org_scope_contract.sql returns violation rows only, plus one summary row `DB-013 staff_members organization scope|t` computed from the same predicates, so an unapplied target cannot pass vacuously. It asserts 9 properties: RLS enabled; the three permissive names absent; no policy on the table carries an unconditional USING or WITH CHECK for a command that takes one; no policy on the table is reachable by anon or PUBLIC; the three scoped policies exist on the right command scoped to authenticated; each scoped policy's predicate contains `org_id is not null`, a `staff_members.org_id` correlation, an `organizations` resolution and a `has_perm` call for the right permission, on WITH CHECK as well as USING where the command has one; staff_members_worker_read_own survives as a SELECT on `user_id = auth.uid()`; the UPDATE policy gates both the existing and the resulting row; and no unreviewed policy beyond the five known names survives. The predicates are matched as PostgreSQL RENDERS them (pg_get_expr prints `FROM organizations` unqualified and `staff_members.org_id` for the correlation), not as they were written, because matching the source spelling would fail against a healthy target. The behavioural half is supabase/tests/db013_staff_members_scope.harness.sh, which measures the cross-tenant read, insert and update BEFORE the migration as a negative control, measures them after, proves null and unresolvable org_id deny, proves the worker own-row and venue employer paths are unchanged, proves the new org path GRANTS as well as denies, then removes a policy and confirms the postflight reports it, then re-introduces read_all_staff ALONGSIDE the scoped policy and confirms the postflight still reports it, then re-applies and confirms green.

recovery.rollback: DROP POLICY staff_members_scoped_read ON public.staff_members; DROP POLICY staff_members_scoped_insert ON public.staff_members; DROP POLICY staff_members_scoped_update ON public.staff_members; - issued as a later forward migration, never as an edit to this file. Rolling back does NOT re-open the exposure on a fully replayed target, because 20260823210000 already dropped the three permissive policies there; it only removes the org-scoped access this migration adds. On a target where 20260823210000 did not run, a rollback WOULD re-open the cross-tenant exposure, which is why the rollback path also has to re-run the equivalent of that migration's drop, and why the preferred recovery for a bad apply is a forward fix, not this rollback.
recovery.forwardFix: Any correction is a new additive migration with a higher version carrying DROP/CREATE POLICY for public.staff_members. The post-state DO block in this file will raise on such a migration's own apply if it leaves an unconditional clause or an anon/PUBLIC-reachable policy behind, so a bad forward fix cannot be applied silently.

queries: SELECT p.polname, p.polcmd, p.polroles::regrole[], pg_get_expr(p.polqual, p.polrelid) AS using_expr, pg_get_expr(p.polwithcheck, p.polrelid) AS check_expr FROM pg_policy p JOIN pg_class c ON c.oid = p.polrelid JOIN pg_namespace n ON n.oid = c.relnamespace WHERE n.nspname='public' AND c.relname='staff_members' ORDER BY p.polcmd, p.polname

-- A CORRECT DENIAL LOOKS LIKE THIS. Run each as a real caller, with that caller's own JWT. (1) cross-tenant read, an account with no membership in the owning org: SELECT count(*) FROM public.staff_members;  -> returns 0. The query SUCCEEDS. 0 rows, not a permission error: the role still holds the table grant, and RLS is what filters the rows. An error here means the grant is missing, which is a different problem.

-- (2) cross-tenant insert, same account: INSERT INTO public.staff_members (name, org_id) VALUES ('probe','<other org uuid>');  -> ERROR 42501: new row violates row-level security policy for table "staff_members". 42501 with that exact message is the correct outcome. 0 rows affected, or success, is a FAILURE.

-- (3) cross-tenant update, same account: UPDATE public.staff_members SET phone='probe' WHERE id='<a row id in the other org>';  -> UPDATE 0. Then SELECT phone FROM public.staff_members WHERE id='<that id>'; -> unchanged. 0 rows is the correct outcome; a changed value is a FAILURE.

-- (4) non-regression, the owning org's own manager: SELECT count(*) FROM public.staff_members;  -> returns the tenant's row count, NOT 0. If this is 0 the apply has over-denied and must be rolled forward, not accepted.
-- (5) non-regression, a worker whose own staff_members row carries their user_id: SELECT count(*) FROM public.staff_members;  -> returns 1 (their own row only) and never the tenant's other rows.

-- (6) fail-closed probe: SELECT count(*) FROM public.staff_members WHERE org_id IS NULL;  -> as any caller, this must never return a row the caller could not otherwise see; for a manager of the owning org it returns 0.
SELECT count(*) AS staff_members_rows, count(*) FILTER (WHERE org_id IS NULL) AS null_org_rows, count(DISTINCT org_id) AS distinct_orgs FROM public.staff_members

verificationOwner: release/ops operator for the staging apply and every probe in postflight.queries; security-admin reviewer for the read/update boundary and for the two findings this lane deliberately did not fix; WFC-003 (CP-102) for the workforce.view / workforce.manage role-matrix gap and the workforce identity contract; orchestrator for routing the other-tables suspect list produced alongside DB-013.
evidence: supabase/tests/db013_staff_members_scope.harness.sh - EXECUTED, ALL CHECKS PASSED, 61 PASS / 0 FAIL, on a throwaway PostgreSQL 16.15 cluster.

The negative control is real, not assumed. With the three permissive policies in place, an authenticated account that is a member of org B only: reads 5 of 5 staff_members rows; INSERTs a row scoped to org A (rc=0); UPDATEs org A's row (1 row) and the harness asserts the write really landed (ROW_ORG.phone became 'pwned') before restoring the fixture. Without that, the after-state would measure nothing.

After the migration, the same account: reads 0 of 5 rows; reads 0 by id; INSERT is rejected with `new row violates row-level security policy for table "staff_members"`; UPDATE matches 0 rows; org A's row is byte-unchanged.

WITH CHECK is proven independently of USING: a workforce.manage member of org A who CAN read org A's row is REJECTED when re-scoping it to org B, and org B is invisible to them under USING (0 rows matched).

Fail-closed is proven for both clauses. NULL org_id: unreadable by a non-member AND by an org A manager. Unresolvable org_id: the harness seeds an org_members row for an organization id that has NO organizations row, with session_replication_role = replica to get past the foreign key, and then ASSERTS that public.has_perm(that user, that org id, 'workforce.manage') IS TRUE before checking that the row is unreadable and unupdatable and that an INSERT with that org_id is rejected. The permission check is true, so the denial can only be coming from the policy's resolution guard - which is the assertion that would be vacuous without the precondition.

Non-regression is proven for both pre-existing access paths, using the chain's own function text extracted BY LINE RANGE at run time (public._tourify_has_columns, public.can_manage_hiring from 20260625000000; public.is_org_member, public.has_perm from 20260821180438; 273 lines extracted) plus the chain's own CREATE TABLE for staff_members (20250818120000:211-229) and the column adds from 20260602120000, 20260625000000 and 20260821031214. A worker still reads exactly their own row; a venue owner still reads AND updates their venue roster row through the untouched staff_members_employer_manage_hiring, and reads 0 org A rows.

The new org path is proven to GRANT, not only to deny: can_manage_hiring(an org A manager, 'organization', org A) is asserted FALSE - it cannot reach a null-employer row - and only then is that same manager shown reading, updating and inserting on org A's rows through the new policies. And workforce.view is proven not to be workforce.manage: the viewer's UPDATE matches 0 rows and their INSERT is rejected 42501, while they still read both of org A's seeded rows.

The postflight is proven able to fail twice, in the two ways that matter: once by removing staff_members_scoped_read, and once by re-introducing read_all_staff WHILE the scoped policy is present. The second is the CP-104 case - a scoped policy and a permissive policy coexisting - which a 'does a scoped policy exist' check scores as safe. Re-applying the migration returns the postflight to green.
Idempotency: applied twice with no error, policy set compared byte-identical before and after.

The harness asserts its own pre-state (5 staff_members policies, 1 carrying an unconditional clause; 5 staff_members rows, 2 organizations, 5 org_members rows) and its own post-state (the exact 5-name surviving policy set, and 0 rows for a cross-tenant caller). A silently failed fixture is the Wave 33 failure shape and every check above would be vacuous without those assertions.

LOCAL EMULATION ONLY: PostgreSQL 16.15, a throwaway cluster in a temp dir, the shared db011 auth/roles bootstrap, and chain function/CREATE TABLE text extracted verbatim by line range. Not Supabase, not a hosted project, not a chain replay, no `supabase db reset`, no `db push --include-all` (CP-051).

NOT PROVEN HERE and required before this is launch-grade: behaviour on a real Supabase target; whether `authenticated` actually holds SELECT on public.organizations there; PostgREST schema-cache refresh; whether the three permissive policies are present or absent on any given target (DB-002's out-of-band application means the chain cannot answer that); whether any consumer reads staff_members through a path this change would alter; and whether `staff_shifts_scoped_read`'s view-only predicate is a second, real instance of the gap the new read policy avoids.
